wine.name: Le Cèdre
wine.grapes: Malbec alone, the grape called Côt or Auxerrois in Cahors.
wine.sites: Cones of limestone scree on the hillsides of Bru at Vire-sur-Lot, and the high Mindel terraces of very old Lot alluvium.
wine.making: Fermented with native yeasts and kept on its skins for about thirty days with gentle extraction, then aged about two years in large oak casks of 57 hectolitres and in 500 litre barrels. By the estate's account nothing is added in the cellar but a little sulphur before bottling.
wine.glass: Black plum, blackberry and violet over cocoa, iris and a smoky, peppery edge; deep in colour and dense, with firm but ripe tannin, fresh acidity and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed in its first years, it wants time in bottle to open, then keeps and deepens for many years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead and an older one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The red only appellation of the Lot, recognised by decree in April 1971, with at least seventy per cent Malbec.
The grape, called Côt or Auxerrois in Cahors; Le Cèdre is Malbec alone.

records.table: Le Cèdre is Château du Cèdre's Cahors of Malbec alone, from limestone scree and high terraces above the Lot, fermented with native yeasts and aged two years in large oak. Dark and dense, with plum, violet and cocoa, it wants decanting and duck or lamb beside it.
records.story: Château du Cèdre began as a mixed farm at Bru, in Vire-sur-Lot, where a couple who grew and distilled lavender planted their first vines in 1958: by the estate's account a massal selection of Malbec, grafted by hand on limestone scree. It was two years after the frost of February 1956 had all but destroyed what was left of the vineyards of Cahors, and in the replanting that followed Malbec, called Côt here, took a larger share. Cahors became an appellation by the decree of 15 April 1971, and in 1973 the couple bottled their first wine, while they went on distilling their lavender beside it. In 1987, when the father fell ill, the couple's two sons came home to take the estate on, and in the years that followed they made its name. Their thinking on organic farming began in the early 1990s, by their own account, and the estate went on to farm organically. Le Cèdre, Malbec alone from the stony hillsides and the old river terraces, is the wine it is known by, and it teaches what modern Cahors is: the black wine of the Lot, ripe and polished, yet firm.

traps: Le Cèdre is Malbec alone; the château wine, Château du Cèdre, adds a little Merlot and Tannat within the appellation's rule of at least seventy per cent Malbec.
Auxerrois in Cahors means Malbec; in Alsace the same name is a white grape related to Pinot Blanc.
Cahors is red only, so the estate's white wines go out under other names, such as Vin de France or IGP Côtes du Lot.

wine.name: Château Montus Cuvée Prestige
wine.grapes: Tannat alone, the principal grape of Madiran.
wine.sites: A selection of the estate's parcels on steep slopes covered in large rounded pebbles over strata of brown and orange clay, at Castelnau-Rivière-Basse in the hills of Madiran.
wine.making: Macerated for three to six weeks and fermented in wooden vats, then raised in new oak barrels, fourteen to sixteen months by the estate's sheet. From the 2017 vintage, by an importer's and a critic's accounts, a further spell of years in large oak casks follows the barrels.
wine.glass: Blackberry and black cherry over graphite, smoke and toasted oak; dark and dense, with massive, grippy tannin, fresh acidity and a long, firm finish that stays tight for years.
wine.ageing: Fiercely tannic when young, it needs ten years or more for its grip to loosen, and a strong vintage keeps for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle two hours ahead and an older one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The red appellation recognised by decree in 1948, with Tannat its principal grape.
The estate's selection of its parcels, Tannat alone, raised first in new oak barrels.

records.table: Château Montus Cuvée Prestige is Madiran at full strength: Tannat alone from steep slopes of rounded pebbles over clay, raised in new oak barrels and, from the 2017 vintage, in large casks after them. Dark, smoky and fiercely tannic, it wants years in bottle and a long decanting.
records.story: Madiran was recognised as an appellation by decree in 1948: a red wine of the South West built on Tannat, a grape known for the weight of its tannin. In 1980 the heir of a Madiran grower family, whose own estate was Château Bouscassé, bought Château Montus at Castelnau-Rivière-Basse, convinced, as the estate tells it, that Tannat had more in it than Madiran had yet shown. The slopes of Montus are steep and covered in large rounded pebbles over clay. With the 1985 vintage he made the first Cuvée Prestige, by the estate's account and others' the first Madiran of Tannat alone raised entirely in new oak barrels, at a time when Madiran was little known outside the South West. The estate tells how it made waves when it did better than many famous French wines at tastings, and the name of Madiran travelled with it. Montus and Bouscassé stayed two estates under one owner, each making red Madiran and white Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh, and the Montus range came to hold Montus XL, kept three years and more in barrel; from the 2017 vintage the pure Tannat wines also spent years in large casks after their new barrels. The Prestige is the bottle to learn Tannat by: pure, dark and tannic, and the wine that showed Madiran could be made for long keeping.

others.name: Montus XL
others.note: Tannat alone, held three years and more in 600 litre demi-muids, by the estate's sheet.

Montus Prestige and Montus XL are separate cuvées of Tannat alone, XL held three years and more in demi-muids; Montus Rouge adds Cabernet Sauvignon.
Montus and Bouscassé are two estates under one owner, not one estate under two names.

The buyer of 1980 is living and is described, never named; Alain Brumont, named in the library's holdings line and in its w- record, is a living name for people.json, for the merge agent. The estate's pages are on the family company's domain, which carries the surname alone.

The plan's why and the library's w- record speak of old vines; the merchants read give vines of about thirty years and the estate a selection of its parcels, so the record says the selection and not old vines.

The present label: the estate's own wine list names Montus Prestige, Montus XL and Montus Rouge as three wines, so the Prestige is current and XL a separate cuvée. One iDealwine page says the Prestige was given up in 2004, and an estate note of 2014 speaks of La Tyre and Prestige going into Montus, yet merchants list Prestige of 2011, 2018 and 2020; worth a refuter's look.

The blind tasting is told without its year or its rank: one merchant gives 1986 and a place among the first three of a field of Bordeaux grands crus, another says it beat them, the estate that it did better than many famous wines.

The first Madiran of Tannat alone raised entirely in new oak rests on the estate's Prestige page and on Sud Ouest France and a Toulouse merchant, hedged as the estate's account and others'. The maceration, the wooden vats and the fourteen to sixteen months in new oak rest on the estate's page and Clos des Millésimes; Montus Rouge's blend and élevage on the estate's Montus Rouge page, read in the same search as its Montus XL page.

Left out for want of a second source: the inheritance of Bouscassé in 1979 (one merchant), the malolactic in new barrels (an importer's copy of the estate's sheet), the slope's aspect towards the Pyrenees, the La Tyre parcel, the nickname of the Pétrus of Madiran (a selling line), and the micro-oxygenation of the 1990s, which the library teaches for Madiran but no source tied to Montus. A wine tourism page says that from 2018 the estate's pure Tannat wines would move from new barrels to three to ten years in large casks; the estate's own Prestige page still gives fourteen to sixteen months in new barrels, which the record follows, and a refuter may wish to try it.

wine.name: Quintessence du Petit Manseng
wine.sites: A narrow, steep valley at Monein facing full south, on clay and silica soil in the foothills of the Pyrenees.
wine.making: Picked by hand in the second half of December, in three or four passes through the vines, from grapes left to shrivel on the vine in sun and frost: passerillage, not noble rot. The must is fermented in new oak barrels and the wine aged in them for about two years.
wine.glass: Candied pineapple, quince paste and candied orange peel over honey and toasted oak; very sweet and full, yet cut by the high, piercing acidity of Petit Manseng, with a long, fresh finish.
wine.ageing: Sweet and vivid when young, it keeps and deepens for decades, its acidity holding the sweetness in line.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass, beside foie gras or a blue cheese.

label.means: The appellation, recognised for its sweet wines in 1936; dry wines, recognised as Jurançon Sec in 1975, add the word sec.
The small berried, thick skinned grape that can hang on the vine into winter and shrivel there.
The estate's sweet wine picked in December, from Petit Manseng alone.

records.table: Quintessence du Petit Manseng is Domaine Cauhapé's sweet Jurançon: Petit Manseng picked at Monein in the second half of December, shrivelled on the vine rather than touched by noble rot, and raised two years in new oak. Pineapple and quince ride a wire of acidity.
records.story: Jurançon, in the foothills of the Pyrenees near Pau, was recognised as an appellation for its sweet wines in 1936, and its dry wines followed as Jurançon Sec in 1975. Its sweetness comes not from noble rot, as in Sauternes, but from passerillage: Petit Manseng, thick of skin, left on the vine into the winter to shrivel in sun and frost. Domaine Cauhapé, at Monein, traces its first vines, by its own account, to 1558, on land then called Caussapé. The domaine was founded in 1980 by a grower of a farming family, largely self taught, who built it up through the 1980s by buying small parcels one after another around a small family vineyard. On part of the vineyard the estate leaves its Petit Manseng for a late harvest, waiting for two or three frosts and the sunny days after them, and from those grapes comes Quintessence, picked in the second half of December in three or four passes and raised two years in new oak. Set beside the dry Jurançon Sec of the same hills, it shows the two faces of the appellation. Quintessence is the classroom proof of passerillage: no botrytis at all, only time, cold and sun on the vine.

Jurançon Sec was recognised apart in 1975, but under the rules of 2011 it is the appellation Jurançon with the word sec; Jurançon alone is the sweet wine.
Petit Manseng gives Jurançon's sweet wines; Gros Manseng is more often the grape of the dry Jurançon Sec.

wine.name: Cuvée Madame
wine.grapes: Muscadelle, the larger part in the vintages recorded, with Sémillon, all of it touched by noble rot.
wine.sites: Chiefly the clay and limestone parcels at the foot of the Tirecul slope at Monbazillac, above the Dordogne south of Bergerac.
wine.making: Picked by hand in successive passes through the vines, often berry by berry, taking only fruit touched by noble rot, from the first day of each pick by the estate's account. It is fermented in new French oak barrels and aged in them for two years and more, and made only in years that allow it.
wine.glass: Mango, candied orange peel and saffron over honey and crystallised apricot; very sweet and dense, held by fresh acidity and a bitter orange edge, with a long, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Rich enough to enjoy young, it deepens over decades in a cool cellar, the fruit turning towards honey and candied peel.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass, beside foie gras, a fruit tart or Roquefort.

label.means: Bergerac's appellation for sweet white wine, among France's six first appellations, of May 1936.
The estate's selection of botrytised fruit, made only in years that allow it.

records.table: Cuvée Madame is Château Tirecul La Gravière's selection of Monbazillac: Muscadelle and Sémillon touched by noble rot, picked often berry by berry above the Dordogne and raised two years in new oak. Made only in good years, it brings mango, saffron and a salty finish.
records.story: Monbazillac, the sweet white of Bergerac across the Dordogne, was among the six appellations that France recognised first, by the decree of 15 May 1936. Tirecul is an old name on its slopes: by the estate's account its vines, crowned by maritime pines, were long counted among the old premiers crus of Monbazillac, and by the end of the eighteenth century the mark of Tirecul La Gravière carried the image of a pine. By the early 1990s the vines had fallen into poor shape. Early in 1992 a couple took them on lease, seeing what the old vines and the soil, never given chemical fertiliser, could do. Their first vintages were praised, as the estate tells it, and in 1997, five years on, they bought the estate and restored its old cellars. They turned to organic farming in 2009, and from 2012 all their wines were certified organic. In years that allow it they make Cuvée Madame: Muscadelle with Sémillon, picked often berry by berry from the first day of each pass through botrytised fruit, and raised two years and more in new oak. It is the bottle that shows Monbazillac can stand beside Sauternes.

others.name: Château Tirecul La Gravière

others.name: Les Pins

traps: Monbazillac lies in Bergerac on the Dordogne, outside the Bordeaux appellations, though it uses the grapes of Sauternes.
Muscadelle is not Muscat: it is a grape of its own, and in Cuvée Madame it is the larger part.
Cuvée Madame is not made every year: it is the estate's selection in years that allow it, beside Château Tirecul La Gravière itself.

The couple are living and are described, never named; Claudie Bilancini and Bruno Bilancini, named in the library's holdings line, are living names for people.json, for the merge agent. The estate's page about them carries their names in its address and is not cited.

Left out for want of a source: the first vintage of Cuvée Madame (1995 is the oldest found; merchants list 1995 to 1999, 2001, 2006, 2009, 2015 and 2021, and one says no 2000), whom Madame names, the yields and the leased area.

The lint's note on the first day of each pick is the estate's method (its page gives Cuvée Madame the grapes of the first day of each botrytis pick), not a claim of rank, and is hedged as its account. No swap proposed: the pick is the estate's flagship by every source read.

wine.name: Mauzac Nature
wine.grapes: Mauzac Rose alone, a pink skinned strain of Mauzac, the old white grape of Gaillac.
wine.sites: The family's vines of the Domaine des Très Cantous at Cahuzac-sur-Vère, on clay and limestone, trained as free standing bush vines in the old Gaillac way.
wine.making: The grapes are pressed straight away, the juice settled for a day and fermented with its own yeasts. When some thirty grams of sugar remain, a filtration slows the fermentation; after two months the wine is bottled and finishes fermenting there, the bubbles forming over about three months, with no sugar or liqueur de tirage added and a little sweetness left.
wine.glass: Yellow and red apple, apple skin and a note of cider over lemon and fresh bread dough; lightly sparkling with fine bubbles, a touch of sweetness and fresh, clean acidity.
wine.ageing: A wine for its youth: drink it within a few years of the harvest, while the apple fruit and the bubbles are fresh.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass or a tulip rather than a narrow flute.

label.means: The appellation of the Tarn, its whites recognised in 1938; its rules allow sparkling wine by the ancestral method.
Mauzac made sparkling by a single fermentation finished in bottle, with no sugar or liqueur added.

records.table: Mauzac Nature is Domaine Plageoles's sparkling Gaillac made the old local way: Mauzac Rose fermented once and bottled before the fermentation ends, so it finishes in bottle with no sugar added. Lightly sparkling, with apple and a touch of sweetness, pour it cool as an aperitif.
records.story: The Plageoles family has worked its vines at Gaillac, on the Tarn, since 1805 by its own account. Gaillac's white wines were recognised as an appellation by the decrees of 21 March 1938, its reds and rosés in 1970, and its rules allow two kinds of sparkling wine: one by a second fermentation in bottle, the other by the ancestral method, called méthode gaillacoise, a single fermentation finished in bottle. Many of Gaillac's old local grapes had all but vanished in the nineteenth century. From the 1970s and through the 1980s the family, father and son, set out to find them again: Ondenc, Prunelart and Verdanel among them came back to their own ground. The estate went on to farm all its vines organically, and a younger generation of the family has since taken up the work. Mauzac Nature, from the pink skinned Mauzac Rose, is made as the old method asks: pressed, fermented with its own yeasts and bottled before the end, so the last of the fermentation makes the bubbles. It teaches the ancestral method in its home, and Mauzac, the old white grape of Gaillac and of Limoux.

others.name: Vin de Voile
others.note: Mauzac aged for years under a veil of yeast, never topped up: a Gaillac rarity kin to vin jaune.

others.name: Ondenc

traps: The ancestral method is one fermentation finished in bottle with no liqueur de tirage; the traditional method of Champagne adds one for a second fermentation.
Mauzac Rose is a strain of the Mauzac grape, not a rosé wine: Mauzac Nature is a white sparkling wine.

cards.front: Domaine Plageoles's Mauzac Nature: how does it get its bubbles?
cards.back: By the ancestral method: one fermentation, bottled before it ends, so it finishes in bottle with no sugar or liqueur added.

cards.front: Which lost Gaillac grapes did the Plageoles family bring back, and since when has it worked there?
cards.back: Ondenc, Prunelart and Verdanel among others; by its own account it has worked its Gaillac vines since 1805.

questions.q: A guest asks how Domaine Plageoles's Mauzac Nature differs from Champagne in the making. What do you say?
opts: One fermentation, finished in bottle, no sugar added
A second fermentation after a liqueur de tirage
Carbon dioxide added to a finished wine
A second fermentation in a sealed tank
questions.exp: The ancestral method bottles the wine before its only fermentation ends, with no liqueur de tirage; Champagne adds one to start a second fermentation in bottle.

questions.q: Which grapes did the Plageoles family set out to bring back to Gaillac from the 1970s on?
opts: Ondenc, Prunelart and Verdanel
Malbec, Merlot and Tannat
Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng
Sémillon, Sauvignon and Muscadelle
questions.exp: The family recovered lost local grapes such as Ondenc, Prunelart and Verdanel; Malbec, Merlot and Tannat are the grapes of Cahors, never lost there.

report: Founded 1805 rests on the estate's own page (the domaine worked since 1805) and merchants' accounts; one names a founder of that year whom no second source names, so nobody of 1805 is named.

The grower who led the recovery of the old grapes is described, never named: no source read reports his death, and one describes him as a sprightly man in his eighties. Living names for people.json, for the merge agent: Robert Plageoles, Bernard Plageoles, Florent Plageoles and Romain Plageoles; the grandfather, Marcel Plageoles, has no dates in any source read and is not named.

The recovery is dated to the 1970s by two accounts (one ties its start to 1970, when Gaillac opened to reds) and to the 1980s by another, so the story says from the 1970s and through the 1980s, father and son.

The library calls the wine's grape Mauzac; the estate's sheet gives Mauzac Rose alone, which the record follows. The library writes Len de l'El, which the record keeps; merchants write Loin de l'Oeil, the same grape.

The making (direct pressing, a day's settling, native yeasts, bottling after about two months) rests on the estate's sheet; the single fermentation with no liqueur de tirage on the INAO's cahier and a merchant's account.

Left out for want of a source: the Vin de Voile's vessel and its years under the veil (one account says seven years in barrels in the oldest cellar, another that the family refuses wood), the residual sugar and strength in figures, and whether the label prints méthode gaillacoise or méthode ancestrale.
